name: Captain Midnight
title: The Night Someone Outgunned HBO From Orbit
claims: On April 27, 1986 a person using the pseudonym Captain Midnight jammed HBO's signal on Galaxy 1 during The Falcon and the Snowman | 1
The message was on screen for 4.5 minutes | 1
The message reached the eastern half of the US, more than half of HBO's 14.6 million subscribers | 1
The message protested HBO's rates for satellite dish owners | 1
Mid-1980s media companies began scrambling signals and charging home dish owners | 1
Starting in the 1970s a small community of enthusiasts, mostly engineers, built dishes and accessed pay TV for free | 1
Accessing the signals was not illegal at the time; restaurant and hotel chains used the technology | 1
HBO began 24-hour scrambling on January 15, 1986 | 1
Another account says scrambling followed a 1984 petition to Congress and began by January 1985, with HBO the first pay-TV service to require a descrambler | 2
HBO offered dish owners a subscription at $12.95 a month, equal to or slightly higher than cable | 1
Another account says dish owners paid about $4 more than cable users | 2
Descrambler cost $395 in one account | 1
Descrambler cost about $500 in another account | 2
Dish owners paid for and serviced their own equipment | 1
Several dish dealers closed stores because of lower dish sales | 1
Industry association members went to Washington in March 1986 to urge Congress to protect access | 1
His dish business declined after scrambling | 1, 2
He cut advertising and switched off air conditioning to save money | 1
He took a part-time operations engineer job at an uplink station in Florida to pay bills | 1
He wrote protest letters to legislators and spent money on awareness | 1
At 12:49 a.m. on April 20 he transmitted a color bar test pattern over HBO's signal | 1
HBO did not investigate because it was overnight and few were watching | 1
On April 26 he was alone at the station after the second engineer left at 6 p.m. | 1
He oversaw the uplink of Pee-wee's Big Adventure for a pay-per-view network | 1
He used color bars and a character generator, and spent a couple of minutes composing the message | 1
The message began with a polite greeting because he did not want to be insulting | 1
He chose the name from a film he had recently seen, unrelated to the radio show | 1
The transmission dish was 30 feet and was swung to aim at Galaxy 1 | 1, 2
Frequencies were widely published in manuals and enthusiast magazines | 1, 2
Message began at 12:32 a.m. EST, about two minutes into the movie, as five lines of white capital letters | 1
Hughes Communications noticed immediately, threatened to shut down HBO's signal or alter the satellite's course, and executives believed the hacker was a domestic terrorist | 1
HBO's technician at Hauppauge, Long Island called Hughes, who had no explanation | 1, 2
The HBO technician raised power from 125 to 2,000 watts and the culprit matched it in a roughly 90-second contest | 1, 2
Higher power risked damaging the satellite, so HBO gave up | 1, 2
He abandoned control and went home, felt guilty, and was surprised to see it on network television | 1
He pretended to know nothing at work and told only close friends, imagining federal agents visiting | 1
FCC chief assembled staff for an emergency meeting eight hours after the intrusion | 1
On April 28 HBO's chairman wrote to the FCC about threatening calls to move Galaxy 1 into another orbit; credibility unknown | 1
More than 200 people called the FBI to falsely confess | 1
One executive called it "video terrorism" | 1, 2
Mother Jones determined three additional satellites could potentially have been taken over: CBS feed, Voice of America, Navy Fleetsatcom 1 | 1
Mother Jones posited hobbyist could hijack satellites that alert the military to Soviet actions, risking nuclear destruction | 1, 2
One account calls the fear a little or a lot of fear-mongering | 2
The FCC had no policies or safeguards to prevent dish owners interfering with transmissions | 2
FBI assisted; DOJ indicated desire to get involved; 100 FCC field offices and monitoring stations involved, with at least six FCC employees | 1
An anonymous tip first led investigators to the Dallas-Fort Worth area | 1
About 2,000 licensed transmitters narrowed to 580 with large enough antennas | 1, 2
Investigators studied footage copies from an FCC engineer and HBO viewers because tape machines were not running | 1
The character generator model was identified; one account says fewer than 100 sites used the typeface | 1, 2
Stations inoperative or transmitting other material were removed, leaving twelve, then three prime suspects | 1
Someone overheard him bragging at a payphone at a Florida rest area and noted his car's license plate | 1
In July investigators spoke to him after he lost his job because the pay-per-view network closed | 1, 2
Two FCC agents and a US Attorney visited with a subpoena two weeks later; he claimed no crime and began to feel evidence was thin | 1
One account says he surrendered, another says he confessed and pleaded guilty | 1, 2
Penalty was $5,000 fine, one year probation, one-year amateur radio license suspension | 1
Alternative was fighting charge with potential $100,000 fines; FCC more interested in learning how he did it | 2
Congress passed a 1986 law making satellite hijacking a felony | 1
The Automatic Transmitter Identification System was developed in response | 1
HBO was never targeted again; business survived the dish downturn and is still operating | 2
In November 1987 a Chicago station's news was hijacked by a man in a Max Headroom mask, who also took over a PBS affiliate; never found | 2

Note: the first lines of the script contain a false start ("twenty-two thousand miles" and "Wait. I should stick..."). Those two lines are not supported by the sources and should be cut before recording. The script should open at "On one night in 1986, two operators fought over a television satellite with nothing but raw power."
